claim: Anthropic's multi-agent system (Claude Opus 4 lead agent + Claude Sonnet 4 subagents) outperformed a single-agent Claude Opus 4 system by 90.2% on Anthropic's internal research evaluation, especially for breadth-first queries requiring multiple independent lines of investigation.
stance_target: Director/Worker multi-agent architectures measurably outperform single-agent systems on parallelizable, open-ended tasks
scope_conditions: Anthropic internal research eval, published June 2025
quoted_support: We found that a multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on our internal research eval.

claim: Multi-agent research systems use approximately 15x more tokens than simple chat interactions, and single agents use about 4x more tokens than chat -- meaning multi-agent architectures are only economically justified for tasks whose value exceeds this token cost multiplier.
stance_target: the whitepaper's cost/resource optimization pillar must account for a 15x token cost multiplier as the baseline economics of multi-agent 'software factory' designs
scope_conditions: Anthropic production token-usage data, published June 2025
quoted_support: In our data, agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats. For economic viability, multi-agent systems require tasks where the value of the task is high enough to pay for the increased performance.

claim: On the BrowseComp evaluation, three factors (token usage, number of tool calls, model choice) explained 95% of performance variance, with token usage alone explaining 80% of the variance -- validating an architecture that distributes work across agents with separate context windows to add parallel reasoning capacity.
stance_target: raw token/compute budget, not just better prompting, is the primary driver of agentic task performance, justifying parallel multi-agent token distribution
quoted_support: In our analysis, three factors explained 95% of the performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation... We found that token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance, with the number of tool calls and the model choice as the two other explanatory factors.

claim: An agent given a flawed MCP tool description was able to test the tool dozens of times, diagnose failure modes, and rewrite its own tool description, resulting in a 40% decrease in task completion time for subsequent agents using the corrected description.
stance_target: agents can perform self-improving skill/tool refinement loops (relevant to the 'Advanced Skill Sequences' pillar) with measurable performance gains
quoted_support: We even created a tool-testing agent—when given a flawed MCP tool, it attempts to use the tool and then rewrites the tool description to avoid failures... this process for improving tool ergonomics resulted in a 40% decrease in task completion time for future agents using the new description.

claim: Parallelizing both subagent spawning (3-5 subagents at once rather than serially) and subagent tool-calling (3+ tools in parallel per subagent) cut total research time by up to 90% for complex queries.
stance_target: parallel execution architecture, not just more capable models, is the primary lever for reducing autonomous agent task latency
quoted_support: For speed, we introduced two kinds of parallelization: (1) the lead agent spins up 3-5 subagents in parallel rather than serially; (2) the subagents use 3+ tools in parallel. These changes cut research time by up to 90% for complex queries.

claim: Anthropic uses rainbow deployments (gradually shifting traffic from old to new agent code versions while both run simultaneously) because stateful, long-running agents cannot all be upgraded atomically without breaking in-flight execution state.
stance_target: continuous-operation infrastructure for long-running autonomous agents requires specialized deployment patterns distinct from stateless service deployment
quoted_support: We can't update every agent to the new version at the same time. Instead, we use rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents, by gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously.

claim: Anthropic's agent evaluation uses a single LLM-as-judge call scoring outputs 0.0-1.0 with a pass-fail grade across five rubric criteria (factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, tool efficiency), found more consistent and human-aligned than using multiple separate judges.
stance_target: rigid evals for multi-agent systems should use a single structured rubric-scoring LLM judge call rather than fragmented multi-judge setups
quoted_support: We experimented with multiple judges to evaluate each component, but found that a single LLM call with a single prompt outputting scores from 0.0-1.0 and a pass-fail grade was the most consistent and aligned with human judgements.

claim: Human evaluation caught a systematic failure mode automated evals missed: early research agents consistently chose SEO-optimized content farms over authoritative but lower-ranked sources like academic PDFs or personal blogs, fixed only by adding explicit source-quality heuristics to prompts.
stance_target: automated/LLM-judge evaluation alone is sufficient for zero-hallucination quality control of agent output source selection
quoted_support: human testers noticed that our early agents consistently chose SEO-optimized content farms over authoritative but less highly-ranked sources like academic PDFs or personal blogs. Adding source quality heuristics to our prompts helped resolve this issue.
